analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from denying coverage or raising premiums based on genetic test results.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee in March 1999 and never received a vote or any further action before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for health insurers to deny enrollment, refuse coverage, or raise premiums based on predictive genetic information — a person's own genetic tests, their family members' tests, or diseases that run in their family. It also would have stopped insurers from demanding genetic information except when actually needed to diagnose, treat, or pay for care, and would have required plans to post confidentiality notices and safeguard genetic data. It applied to both employer group plans and individually purchased insurance.
analysis.who_benefits: People who carry genetic risk — for themselves or in their family — including the many who avoided genetic testing for fear an insurer would use the results against them. The bill would have let them get tested and counseled without risking their coverage or their premiums.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with genetic disease risk in their families

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans and insurers from restricting enrollment or adjusting premiums for a group based on predictive genetic information about any member or their family, including the fact that someone sought genetic services [S2] [S3].
In the individual insurance market, bars insurers from using predictive genetic information as a condition of eligibility or in setting a person's premium rate [S3].
Stops plans and insurers from requesting or requiring predictive genetic information, except that they may request (never require) it for diagnosis, treatment, or payment purposes [S2] [S3].
Requires plans to give written notice of their confidentiality practices and to maintain administrative, technical, and physical safeguards for genetic data [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers sponsoring group plans, who would lose the ability to use genetic information in underwriting and would bear the cost of compliance — confidentiality notices, data safeguards, and a larger risk pool that includes people with genetic predispositions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and group plan sponsors

drawbacks.text: Restricting pricing to 'groups' rather than individuals still allowed the group's overall premium to reflect claims experience, so costs from people with genetic risk could spread to co-workers rather than disappear [S3].

Insurers argued that if people can learn their genetic risk while insurers cannot, sicker people enroll and premiums rise for everyone in the pool — the standard adverse-selection objection to any underwriting restriction (general policy mechanism, not in the sources).

The bill covered health insurance only; it did nothing about genetic discrimination in hiring and employment, which was the other major fear of people considering genetic tests — a gap that took a separate law to close years later (general knowledge, not in the sources).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was real and concrete: without this protection, people with a family history of diseases like breast cancer or Huntington's had a financial reason to avoid genetic testing, and those who tested positive could face denial of coverage or unaffordable premiums in the individual market. The cost — somewhat less precise insurance pricing and compliance burdens for insurers — was modest by insurance-industry standards. The bill's main design weakness was what it left out: employment discrimination, which meant someone could be insured but still fear for their job.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Olympia Snowe introduced the bill on March 4, 1999, joined by six Republican cosponsors including Senator Bill Frist, a physician [S1] [S4] [S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or any other action followed before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers came out ahead: with no law enacted, they kept full discretion to use genetic information in underwriting for two more years, and the people with genetic risk the bill would have protected got no relief. Congress later enacted a broader version, covering jobs as well as insurance, in 2008 (general knowledge, not in the sources).

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers kept their underwriting discretion

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored entirely by Republicans — the senator from Maine and seven colleagues — and no recorded vote or floor opposition ever occurred, so the partisan shape of the full Senate is unknown; the recorded obstacle was inaction in committee, whose chairman was himself a cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill would have barred insurers from denying coverage or setting premiums using predictive genetic information in both group and individual markets, and from demanding genetic tests. Without it, they kept the ability to price and screen based on genetic risk, which is exactly the practice that made people afraid to get tested.

Self-insured and insured group plans would have faced new limits on using genetic information about employees and covered family members, plus confidentiality-notice and data-safeguard requirements. Compliance costs were modest but real.

By removing the insurance penalty for learning one's genetic risk, the bill would have made people far more willing to take genetic tests and seek genetic counseling. Patients and testing providers shared the same interest here.
